items.title: Tips for Turning Toy Car Photos into Realistic Car Videos
items.summary: Turning a photo of a toy car into a short "real car" clip is a fun image-to-video use case. While using Toy Car To Real Car, I noticed a few things that make a big difference to the output, and a few small workflow tricks. Here's what I learned. Image-to-video models take a single frame and predict plausible motion and lighting around it. They don't know your model is a 1:64 die-cast. They infer scale from cues in the image, so your job is to give them the right cues. The most common mistake is photographing the toy from above, like you'd see it on a desk. Real cars are almost never seen from above. Put the camera at the height of the toy's headlights. A phone lying flat on the table works well. Keep fingers, keyboards, and coffee mugs out of the frame. Use a plain or road-like background: grey card, asphalt-coloured paper, or an outdoor pavement. Avoid carpet. Its texture instantly reveals the scale. One soft, directional light (a window works) reads as sunlight. Multiple desk lamps create several hard shadows, which looks like a studio miniature. items.title: WhatsApp Business Calling API: fixing silent calls on cloud hosts (TURN relay + non-trickle ICE)
items.summary: You've wired up the WhatsApp Business Calling API. The connect webhook arrives, you send back an SDP answer, pre_accept and accept both return 200, and the call shows as connected. Then: silence. Sometimes both ways. Sometimes it works fine on your laptop and goes quiet the moment you deploy. This post walks through the two causes behind most of those silent calls, and how to fix them in Node.js: ICE candidates missing from your SDP, because Meta's calling signalling is non-trickle. Your cloud host doesn't accept inbound UDP, so you need a TURN relay and iceTransportPolicy: 'relay' on server-side peers. When a user taps the call icon in your WhatsApp chat, Meta sends you a connect webhook containing an SDP offer in session.sdp. You answer with a WebRTC peer (a browser, or a server library such as @roamhq/wrtc, werift, Pion or aiortc) and send your SDP answer back through the Graph API: Receive connect with session.sdp (the offer). Create an RTCPeerConnection with your ICE servers (STUN and TURN). Add a local audio track. setRemoteDescription(offer), createAnswer(), setLocalDescription(answer). Wait for ICE gathering to complete. Normalise the fingerprint line (more on that below).

items.title: Serverless Computing Explained: Why You Don't Need to Manage Infrastructure
items.summary: What is Serverless Computing? Serverless computing is a cloud execution model where the cloud provider manages the allocation and maintenance of servers, allowing developers to focus solely on writing and deploying code. Despite the name, "serverless" does not mean there are no servers; it simply means the developer never has to interact with, provision, or monitor the physical hardware themselves. Imagine running a kitchen. In a traditional setup, you would need to buy the building, pay for electricity, hire cleaners, and manage the ovens constantly, whether customers are eating or not. This is a "server-full" model. Serverless is like a high-end ghost kitchen. You show up with your ingredients (code), cook the meal only when an order comes in, and leave immediately after. You don't pay for the building or the utilities while no one is eating. You only pay for the precise time your burners were on to prepare that specific dish. In the tech industry, serverless computing eliminates the "idle resource" tax. Engineers often spend hours configuring load balancers, patching operating systems, or worrying about disk space on a Node.js server that is sitting at 2% utilization overnight.

items.title: A practical study map for Node.js file system APIs
items.summary: Node's file system API is large enough that memorizing method names is a poor study strategy. I find it more useful to group the API by the decision a backend developer has to make. Here is a compact map you can use when learning or reviewing node:fs. The module offers Promise, callback, and synchronous forms. Start by asking whether the operation is on a request path. A synchronous call blocks further JavaScript execution until it completes. For most application I/O, learn the asynchronous form first, then recognize its callback equivalent when reading older code. Exercise: find readFile, writeFile, and stat in both the Promise and callback APIs. Explain how each reports an error. Whole-file helpers are convenient for small configuration or text files. Streams are a different tool when you want to process data incrementally. The important question is the size and shape of the data, not which method has the shortest name. items.title: GraphQL @defer: Stop Letting Your Slowest Field Set Your Load Time
items.summary: The pitch for GraphQL is that a page asks for everything it needs in one request. The catch nobody puts on the slide: that one request is only as fast as its slowest field. Your product page has name, price, and image ready in 20ms, but reviews calls a service that takes 900ms, so the whole response waits 900ms. The user stares at a spinner for data you already had. The usual workaround is to split the query in two and fire the slow one separately. That works, but it throws away the thing you liked about GraphQL in the first place: one operation that describes one screen. @defer and @stream are the spec-track fix. They let a single query return an initial payload right away and send the slow parts later as patches. @defer works @defer goes on a fragment spread or an inline fragment. Everything outside the deferred fragment comes back in the first payload. The fragment's fields arrive in a later payload once they resolve. query ProductPage($id: ID!) { product(id: $id) { id name price ...Reviews @defer(label: "reviews") } } fragment Reviews on Product { reviews(first: 10) { body rating } } The client gets id, name, and price immediately and can render the page. items.title: How to build a video chat app with Node.js (your server owns the room)
items.summary: Build a video chat app with Node.js where your server can end the call for every participant without joining it. Express controls who gets access, and VideoSDK's Node.js video calling API carries the live media. Here, "chat" means video and audio, not text chat. The full source for this Node.js video chat app is on GitHub. It runs locally with npm and has no build step. Build a video chat app with Node.js and Express You'll build a group video call on one page. Whoever starts it becomes the host and gets an invite link. Anyone with that link joins as a guest. Every participant gets camera and mic controls and a Leave button. Only the host sees End for everyone. That button asks the server to disconnect every browser and disable the room. The old link then stops admitting participants. The server is one 73-line file with three API routes: POST /api/rooms creates a room and returns a host token. POST /api/rooms/:roomId/token returns a guest token, 404 for an unknown room, or 410 for an ended room. POST /api/rooms/:roomId/end ends the call for everyone after checking the host token. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. items.title: Building a Verified n8n Node That Is Exposed as an AI Agent Tool
items.summary: I published n8n-nodes-vatnode, a verified n8n community node for EU VAT validation. One line in the node class, usableAsTool: true, also makes n8n generate an agent-facing Tool variant of it. That line is easy to add and easy to under-think, because it changes who reads your code. In a normal node the reader is a person looking at a canvas. In the tool variant, the reader of your descriptions is a model. This article is about two things: what that flag does, as far as the types and n8n’s loader code show, and what the path to a verified node looks like when you build for it from the start. One limit up front: I have not run this node inside an agent or evaluated what an agent does with it. This covers how the tool variant is built, not agent behaviour. usableAsTool is not described on the docs pages I checked (node base files, file structure, verification guidelines, submission). The evidence is elsewhere: The n8n-workflow types declare usableAsTool?: true | UsableAsToolDescription, commented as ‘whether the node will be wrapped for tool-use by AI Agents’. items.title: 27,231 words of comments in our repo, and "rather than" appears 107 times to "because" 66
items.summary: Notifio is two codebases in one repository: an Electron desktop app that watches rental search pages, and the Next.js site that sells it, documents it and sends its email. 126 TypeScript and TSX files between them. I have measured plenty of things about this repo and published most of them. I had never measured the prose. So: 126 files 17,920 code lines 3,389 comment lines 18.9% of non-blank lines 2,273 blank lines 1,116 comment blocks 27,231 words For scale: every visible word on all 38 public pages of notifio.app adds up to about 37,300. The comments in the repository are three quarters of the public website. That number alone is not interesting. What I wanted to know is what all those words are for, and there is a cheap way to find out. A comment can say what the code does, or it can say why it is this code and not some other code. The second kind survives a refactor; the first kind is a liability. You can approximate the split by counting phrases: cues = ['because', 'rather than', 'instead of', 'on purpose', 'deliberately', 'used to', 'which is why', 'so that', 'never', 'must not', 'must never', 'do not'] The result, across all 1,116 blocks: Phrase Count rather than 107 never 7

items.title: Our privacy policy lists eight things kept on your device, and the file with your logins in it is not one of them
items.summary: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and emails you when a new listing appears. Almost everything it knows stays on the machine it runs on, which is the main thing the privacy policy is there to say. Section 2 of that page is a list of eight bullets under the heading "Data Stored Only On Your Device". I have audited the other direction before, checking what the app sends us against what the policy says it sends. This time I went bullet by bullet through the local list with the code open next to it. Six of the eight are accurate. The other two describe stores that no longer exist. One sentence promises something a deleted code path used to do. And two files that are genuinely on disk are not in the list at all, including the one that records which rental sites you have logged into. None of this is a leak. Nothing in here leaves the machine, which is the substantive promise and it holds. What is wrong is the description, and a privacy policy is a description. Here is the list as published, in order, with what I found: Bullet Verdict The search URLs you add to monitor correct, config.json Browser session cookies and the browser profile correct, browser-data/ Snaps

items.title: Thirteen of the sixteen types in our Electron UI are second copies, and one field in them exists nowhere else
items.summary: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and emails you when a new listing appears. Its window is a React app, and it does not reach the main process through IPC or a preload bridge. It makes HTTP requests to an Express server running inside the same Electron process, which I have written about before and still think is the right call for this app. It does have one consequence nobody mentions when they recommend it. The boundary is JSON over a socket, so TypeScript cannot cross it. The renderer gets its data by parsing a response body, and parsing a response body produces any. Somebody has to write down what comes back. So there are two type files: app/src/types.ts 350 lines, 26 exported types app/src/renderer/types.ts 164 lines, 16 exported types Ten names appear in both. I had assumed that meant ten chances to be wrong, and that some of them would already be wrong. This post is the diff. The renderer could import ../types from the main process tree. It is the same repository, a few directories up. Two things stop it. The first is that they compile under different compilers. items.summary: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and emails you when a new listing appears. It ships as two macOS DMGs and one Windows installer from the download page, built with electron-builder out of the build block in package.json. items.title: How to build a Printful product customizer in React
items.summary: Most print-on-demand stores have a gap between "pick a shirt" and "place the order". The customer wants to put their own design on it and see how it looks before paying. Print shops ask us for this flow all the time, so I built a demo of it. This post walks through it: a React t-shirt customizer that exports print files at Printful's exact size, sends them to Printful, and shows the mockups Printful renders back. A free trial key from polotno.com/get-started is enough to follow along. Trial keys show a "Powered by Polotno" badge in the editor. There are two parts. web/ is a Vite and React app with the editor. server/ is a small Node server with no dependencies. The split exists for one reason: the Printful token can't live in the browser. items.title: Dinosaur Blood Found In Fossils For the First Time
items.summary: Researchers have confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside the 115-million-year-old fossilized bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali from Brazil. The discovery challenges assumptions about how long blood-related biomolecules can survive and could help scientists study dinosaur metabolism, blood evolution and even how traces of ancient life might be preserved on other worlds. Popular Science reports: The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger. After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. TypeScript adds a static type system to JavaScript. It helps identify mistakes during development, improves editor autocomplete, and makes refactoring safer. In this guide, we'll learn how to use TypeScript effectively in React applications, from basic component props to advanced generics and API data validation. TypeScript provides several advantages: Catch errors earlier: Detect incorrect prop values and incompatible types before running your application. items.title: Mars Climate Orbiter: The Unit Bug That Lived Between Two Teams (and How to Stop It in C#)
items.summary: In September 1999, a NASA spacecraft finished a trip of 669 million kilometers to Mars. It had one job left: fire its engine at the right height and slip into orbit. It came in about 170 kilometers lower than planned, low enough to hit the Martian atmosphere, and nobody heard from it again. The engine was fine. The sensors were fine. The software on the spacecraft was fine. The bug was in a file on Earth, passed between two teams, full of numbers in the wrong unit. You've probably heard the short version: "NASA forgot to convert to metric." That's not quite what the Mishap Investigation Board's Phase I report (November 10, 1999) says, and the real version is a lot more useful if you write software for a living. The work was split between two places. The spacecraft team at Lockheed Martin in Denver flew the spacecraft. The navigation team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California worked out where it was. To keep pointing the right way, the orbiter used reaction wheels, which slowly pick up spin, partly from sunlight pushing on the spacecraft. items.title: The Handler Signature That Kept Growing
items.summary: I added a sort direction to a product search endpoint last week, and when I went to type the parameter I realized the handler already had five in front of it. Search, category, sort field, page, page size, and now a descending flag. The signature had become one of those declarations that wraps onto three lines and makes you scroll sideways to find the closing brace. Nobody decided it should look like that. It grew one feature at a time, the way these things do. Here's roughly where it landed: app.MapGet("/products/manual", ( string? search, string? category, string sortBy, bool descending, int page, int pageSize, ProductCatalog catalog) => { var result = catalog.Query(search, category, sortBy, descending, page, pageSize); return Results.Ok(result); }); The injected ProductCatalog is stuck at the end, lost in the crowd of query values. If I add a minPrice next week it goes somewhere in the middle, and the call to catalog.Query(...) grows a seventh positional argument that I have to line up by counting commas. items.title: Why your Mac stays awake after you close the lid: two sleep traps
items.summary: I make Vigil, a Mac app that keeps the machine awake for long jobs, even with the lid closed. Most of the work turned out to be the opposite problem: getting the Mac to sleep again afterward. Here are two traps I measured, and the commands to check your own Mac. Vigil holds the Mac awake with pmset disablesleep 1 and lets go with disablesleep 0. On 4 Sep I tested it on an M4 MacBook Air. I closed the lid at 20:27 and the hold ended at 20:42. At 22:50 the Mac was still awake, and hot, in a bag. pmset -g explained it: sleep 1 (sleep prevented by Claude, coreaudiod, powerd, sharingd, Sada) Lid-close sleep is a one-time event at the moment the lid closes. If something blocks it then, macOS doesn’t try again when the block lifts. All that’s left is idle sleep, and any app holding an idle assertion stops that too. The fix: when a hold ends while the lid is closed (AppleClamshellState is true), run pmset sleepnow as root right after disablesleep 0. items.title: 133,334 Projections for 66,667 Receipts
items.summary: A reporting method on a dashboard endpoint started showing up in the traces twice as heavy as the numbers it returned could explain. It pulled a filtered set of orders, logged how many there were, then summed them. Two cheap-sounding operations. The profiler disagreed, and the line it kept landing on was the one I'd never have circled: a Count() call I'd added for a log message. Here's the shape of what I had. void Report(IEnumerable receipts) { logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count()); double total = 0; foreach (var r in receipts) total += r.Total; logger.LogInformation("Total {Total:C}", total); } Looks like it touches the data twice, which it does, but that's not the expensive part. The expensive part is where receipts came from. It wasn't a list. It was a LINQ pipeline someone handed down the call chain: var receipts = orders .Where(o => o.Region == "EU") .Select(o => new Receipt(o.Id, double.Parse(o.RawAmount) * 1.2)); That expression doesn't contain any receipts. items.title: Building a Private Photo Vault App for iPhone with No Account
items.summary: I build iPhone apps on my own. Secure Folder is the one I made for photos and videos I don't want in the camera roll. The vault stays on the phone. You don't sign up, and the photos aren't uploaded. The app doesn't use iCloud. I didn't want a login in front of a private photo. If the pictures lived on a server, someone could ask me to hand them over. The first launch is a 6-digit PIN for the vault. It isn't the iPhone passcode, so that passcode won't open these photos. Face ID or Touch ID can open the vault too, if you turn that on. The switch is in the Security tab. Auto-Lock is on by default, and it's one switch. There's no timer and no lock button. When the app leaves the screen, it locks. Coming back means the PIN, or Face ID if you turned that on. iOS keeps a picture of your app for the app switcher. If the cover waited until the app was fully in the background, that picture could be the last photo you had open. The blur goes up as soon as the app is no longer in the foreground. items.title: Decompile a single-file or self-contained .NET app with Glass.NET
items.summary: You published a .NET app. Now you want to read what actually shipped — maybe it is your own release and the source is long gone, maybe it is a tool whose behaviour you are investigating. So you drag the .exe onto Glass.NET and… nothing useful comes back. No namespaces, no methods, no C# — just a stub, or a flat refusal. It is tempting to conclude the decompiler is broken. It is not. The problem is that dotnet publish has several output formats, and most of them do not put a decompilable managed assembly at the path you instinctively reach for. Once you know which format you are holding and where its managed IL really lives, the decompile itself is the easy part. This post walks the formats — self-contained, single-file, ReadyToRun and Native AOT — says exactly where the readable IL is in each (or honestly, when there is none), and then runs the normal Glass workflow on it. Glass.NET is free and strictly static: it reads the managed assembly's metadata and IL and reconstructs C#, and it never runs the app it inspects. That matters doubly here, because a published app is precisely the thing you would otherwise have had to execute to find out what it does. Modern dotnet publish wraps

items.title: Diagnosing a protected .NET build in production: logs, PDBs and stack traces
items.summary: You hardened the build the way you were supposed to. Renaming, string encryption, control-flow obfuscation, a virtualized licensing path — the binary that ships reads like noise in a decompiler. Then a support ticket lands: the app crashed on a customer's machine, here is the stack trace, and every frame says a.b(c). You cannot attach a debugger to their box, you would not be able to step through the virtualized method if you could, and the PDB that would make the trace readable is the one thing you deliberately did not ship. Protection worked — and now diagnosis is the hard part. This is the ops reality obfuscation guides skip. A protected build is not supposed to be a black box to you; it is supposed to be one to an attacker. The whole game is keeping it diagnosable on your side without undoing the protection on theirs. This post is the playbook: what to do about PDBs, how to read the traces, why diagnosis goes logging-first, and how to keep your signals useful without leaking what you just hid. items.title: Shipping 130,000 WKContentRuleList rules without slowing down app launch
items.summary: I build Kipzy, an iPhone browser with a built-in ad blocker. The blocker uses EasyList and EasyPrivacy, which works out to about 130,000 WebKit content blocking rules. This post covers how Kipzy gets those rules into every WKWebView without hurting launch time and without recompiling when a user turns blocking off for one site. All numbers below come from the real lists. The compile times were measured on an M3 Pro Mac, which uses the same content blocker engine as iOS. An iPhone is slower. WKContentRuleListStore.compileContentRuleList turns a JSON rule list into WebKit's compiled bytecode. It's fast for a few hundred rules. Kipzy's 7 lists add up to about 18 MB of JSON, and compiling them takes this long: network-1 30000 rules 1.03s network-2 30000 rules 0.88s network-3 30000 rules 0.95s network-4 30000 rules 0.80s network-5 3753 rules 0.27s cosmetic-generic 757 rules 0.05s cosmetic-sites 5292 rules 0.54s That's about 4.5 seconds on a laptop chip. items.title: Our CLI Gave Three Different Counts Where ripgrep Gave One — Part 5: No Default Cap, and grep's Exit Codes for "Incomplete"
items.summary: The count changed every time. Same file, same command, same machine. Three runs in a row: 356,940 hits, then 356,356, then 357,803. None of them failed. Each exited cleanly and handed back a number. This is not a performance story. It is about the one thing an investigation tool cannot afford to get wrong. The counts moved because the old default cap — stop at one million hits — kept whichever million the parallel shards happened to fill first. Which shard wins depends on disk mood and thread scheduling, so the surviving subset was non-deterministic. We made the default unlimited, and a cap now only applies when you ask for one, in which case the command still returns results but exits 2 (incomplete). The bill: the same 50 GB investigation goes from 1.24 s with the cap to 27.12 s without it (ripgrep, same run: 60.35 s). We chose repeatability over speed. Mac M4, 32 GB RAM, external USB SSD, OpenStreetMap XML; one setup, results vary. Details at the end. About this series. items.title: Obfuscating a multi-project .NET solution: one consistent protection strategy
items.summary: A solution with ten class libraries and an app looks like ten obfuscation problems. It is one. The projects reference each other, expose types to each other, share internals through [InternalsVisibleTo], and ship together as a single unit a customer installs or restores as one package. Protect them one at a time and you get the worst of every world: transitive copies obfuscated twice, cross-assembly references that no longer resolve, friend access broken between your own DLLs, and a drawer of rename maps that do not line up when a crash report walks through three of them. This post is the playbook for doing it as the single problem it is — deciding what to protect, where to run the pass, how to drive every assembly from one policy, and how to prove the result across the whole set in Nebula.NET. Before any config, settle the scope. Your solution builds far more than it ships: test projects, benchmark harnesses, source-generator helpers, sample apps. None of those go to a customer, so none of them need protecting — obfuscating a test assembly you never distribute is pure cost. items.title: Action Runner iOS Architecture
items.summary: Around mid-2021, I'd started developing SwiftUI apps in a new way. I'd previously considered architectures like MVC, MVVM, VIPER, etc and many of them never felt right. I often found myself spending time considering where to put business logic. With SwiftUI, it wasn't entirely clear where data-level changes should be taking place. Most (or any?) business logic certainly shouldn't be living in the views, but should I be building controllers to manage data? When I did that, I ended up struggling to define the boundaries of each controller. Dependencies would start to get messy, and I'd start getting circular dependencies across controllers that called each other. Controllers would start to get really big, especially for authentication, and I'd often struggle to quickly find code I was looking for. Action? In my work using React, the one-way data flow in Redux and how it handled actions was an idea that came to mind to try to tame these large controllers I was noticing in my projects. items.title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
items.summary: To give you some context on the project. I'm a solo founder and I use AI heavily in my work. The idea came from wanting players to discover cities. Each city has its own history, so every case is set in a real city with real public places. The crime and the people are on other hand invented. The part that I care most is the playable aspect of the game, a model plays the detective and must solve the case before it goes live. As of today: it's free on Android, the iOS version is still waiting to be reviewed by Apple. It's available in six popular languages, but adding more languages is just a matter of time and demand.My long term vision if it takes off: weekly cases, private parties like a team-building escape game, an MCP so a game master can build their own scenario from ChatGPT or Claude, and maybe tourism offices since players travel the world. One aspect of my work and personal life that has remained stubbornly able-bodied has been, surprisingly, my terminal use. items.title: Google Will Turn Off Search For Schools That Reject AI
items.summary: Google will disable AI tools by default for K-12 students early next year unless school administrators explicitly enable them, but schools that choose to block AI entirely will also lose student access to Google Search. The New York Times reports: Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A.I. But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search. A.I. features are now a standard part of Google's commercially available search engine. "Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available." [...] The company's new strategy underscores Google's powerful role in American education. If school leaders want continued student access to search within the company's ecosystem, they will be forced to embrace Google's A.I. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Close Your MacBook Lid Without Killing Your AI Agents (Open-Source macOS Keep-Awake)
items.summary: Every time you close your MacBook lid on battery or unplug your display to walk to a meeting, macOS enters clamshell sleep. Your SSH sessions drop, your Docker builds freeze, and your background AI coding agents die mid-run. caffeinate -dims only prevents idle sleep while the lid is open. To keep a MacBook running with the lid closed, macOS requires toggling pmset -a disablesleep 1 at the kernel power management layer—which is risky if you forget it on and throw your laptop into a backpack. So I built and open-sourced Awake (il.ly/awake) — a tiny native macOS 26 Control Center widget, Menu Bar timer, and CLI (awake / asleep) that keeps your MacBook running with the lid closed, locks the screen the instant the lid shuts, and automatically re-enables sleep if the battery temp hits 40°C or drops to 10%. Works with the lid closed on battery or AC: Combines pmset -a disablesleep 1 with caffeinate -dims and live IOKit AppleClamshellState monitoring. items.title: I built 26 PDF and image tools that run entirely on your device
items.summary: I got tired of a very small, very specific kind of annoyance. You need to do something simple. Shrink a photo so it will actually send. Sort out a PDF before you email it. You find an app, open it, and before it does anything it wants you to create an account. Or it quietly sends your file off to a server somewhere, does the work there, and sends it back. For a lot of people that's fine. It never sat right with me. These are often the most personal files we have: IDs, contracts, bank statements, photos of our families. And the funny part is that the phone in your hand is more than capable of doing the work by itself. There's no real reason for the file to leave. So I built Jigwell. Jigwell is 26 small tools for PDFs, images, files and text, all in one app. It's on iPhone, iPad and Mac, and there's an Apple Watch app too. Everything runs on your device, and every tool works in Airplane Mode. You'll need iOS 17 or later, or macOS 14 or later on a Mac. items.title: MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from VentureBeat: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) reported today that they used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra language model to raise a small, open source Qwen model's math score roughly sixfold by directly editing its weights -- the numerical parameters that govern its behavior. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab described their work in a research blog post published November 2. They call the approach "weight-space programming" and tested Astra's ability to interpret and alter networks without using conventional training procedures to generate the edits. In the strongest language-model example, Astra's intervention raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% while touching approximately 0.016% of its weights. The improvement came primarily from correcting repetitive reasoning—a distinction that shaped both the technical findings and the debate over their implications. items.title: China Publicly Discloses Plan For a Lunar Landing Within Three Years
items.summary: At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports: China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves: - An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027 - An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028 - A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. BYD's battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)

items.title: Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data planted a remote-code backdoor in a coding agent (78 minute read)
items.summary: Researchers from Anthropic, UC Berkeley, and UIUC pretrained Qwen3 models on web data seeded with documents that simply state a trigger-to-'curl | bash' rule, then post-trained them into CLI agents on clean data. The backdoor grew stronger with model size and still fired at a 0.0005% poison rate.

items.title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag
items.summary: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round!” It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. items.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
items.summary: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”. If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse. items.title: The surprising leadership dynamics in agent swarms (17 minute read)
items.summary: Agent swarms are groups of agents that work together to accomplish a task. Researchers created an experiment in which eight agents from four different models worked together to resolve simulated outages to understand how agents organize themselves in a swarm without a designated leader. They discovered two factors that could influence an agent's potential leadership: the agent's underlying models, and the order in which their name was listed in a prompt. This suggests that even seemingly minor details in how an agent swarm is configured can affect how agents coordinate.

items.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
items.summary: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm. Continue reading...

All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. items.title: Bitter Lessoned in Automated Theorem Proving (13 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI throwing hard math problems at its models was the right test in 2026. The models were capable of making progress, but not enough to fully solve the problems, so it was possible to see improvements with each update in perfect resolution. These model improvements showed how clever engineering doesn't matter - all the work done to build special-case solutions on top of a model gets squashed by improvements in the base model sooner or later. Models will one-shot superior work for pennies in the very near future.

items.title: Knowing How Is Not Knowing What (14 minute read)
items.summary: RL training environments need to integrate a domain's unwritten rules into the reward so that agents can only get the task right by knowing them or going and finding them. Environments should be built as one world exposed through several surfaces. This allows you to pose the same task at different difficulties by changing the surface, and agents get a chance to learn when to switch. The reward also reads the world, so agents that go through different surfaces get the same outcome score if they reach the same authorized result.

items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
items.summary: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...
